title: Is Bitcoin A Hedge Against Central Banking? Evidence from AI-Driven Monetary Policy Expectations
summary: This paper investigates how monetary policy narratives transmit to Bitcoin prices, introducing a high-frequency Monetary Policy Expectations (MPE) index built from LLM classification of 118,000+ market messages. The study finds that hawkish narratives consistently trigger negative Bitcoin price responses independent of actual Fed rate adjustments, and that the MPE index Granger-causes Bitcoin returns at short-to-medium horizons.
key_points: Authors introduce a high-frequency Monetary Policy Expectations (MPE) index using LLM-based hawkish/dovish classification of 118,000+ market messages
LSTM-SHAP framework reveals non-linear, macroeconomic regime-dependent interactions between policy expectations and Bitcoin
MPE index Granger-causes Bitcoin returns at short-to-medium horizons, establishing linear predictive causality
Bitcoin acts as a sensitive barometer of central bank signaling rather than primarily tracking actual interest rate changes
LLM-derived sentiment is proposed as a leading macroeconomic indicator for the digital asset landscape
Results hold independently of actual Federal Funds Rate adjustments
why_it_matters: This research provides directional evidence that Bitcoin is sensitive to monetary policy narratives, not just realized rate changes. The paper suggests that LLM-derived sentiment measures could potentially serve as indicators for understanding crypto market dynamics. The finding that ex-ante expectations may matter more than ex-post implementation challenges assumptions about Bitcoin as a pure inflation hedge, though specific quantitative thresholds and practical trading applications require full paper review.
macro_context: The paper connects monetary policy expectations (a macro catalyst) to Bitcoin price dynamics, suggesting that Fed communication hawkishness affects crypto markets even when policy rates remain unchanged. This has implications for how macro catalysts should be monitored in digital asset contexts. The regime-dependent findings imply that the same policy signal may have different transmission strength depending on macroeconomic conditions.
